samples.text:
In recent years, a lot of people have moved from the countryside to big cities because they want to find a job. Because of this, many cities become overcrowded. In this essay I will explain the problems which this causes and some measures to deal with them.

The main problem of overcrowding is housing. When too many people come to the city, there is not enough houses for everyone, so the rent becomes very expensive. Many poor people have to live in small rooms or in slums with bad conditions, where there is no clean water. Another problem is traffic. The roads are full of cars and buses, and people spend a long time to go to work every day. Also, the air pollution is increasing because of so many vehicles, and this is bad for people health.

There are several measures that government can take. First, they should build more cheap apartments for low-income workers, so they do not need to live in slums. Second, the public transport must be improved. If there are more metro lines and buses, less people will use their own cars and the traffic will be reduced. In addition, the government can create jobs in the rural areas, for example by building factories or supporting farmers. In this way, young people will not need to move to the city to find a work.

In conclusion, overcrowding in cities causes problems such as expensive housing, traffic jams and pollution. I believe that the government should build cheap housing, improve transport and develop the countryside, because this will make life better for everyone.
samples.why: Addresses problems and measures · relevant but general ideas with limited development · clear paragraphs with basic linking (First, Second, Also) · adequate vocabulary · frequent article and agreement errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
The steady movement of people from rural areas to cities in search of employment has left many urban centres struggling to cope with their growing populations. This essay will examine the main difficulties that overcrowding creates and suggest some measures that could ease them.

Perhaps the most serious problem is the shortage of affordable housing. As demand for accommodation rises faster than new homes can be built, rents increase sharply, and many newcomers on low wages are forced into cramped, poorly maintained buildings or informal settlements that lack basic services such as sanitation. Overcrowding also places enormous pressure on infrastructure. Roads become congested, public transport is packed at peak times and hospitals and schools are often unable to serve everyone, which lowers the quality of life for long-term residents as well as new arrivals.

To deal with these issues, governments need to act on two levels. Within cities, authorities should invest in large-scale social housing and expand public transport networks, for example by building new metro lines that connect affordable suburbs with business districts. This would allow people to live further from the centre without spending hours commuting. However, such measures only address the symptoms, therefore it is also important to reduce the pressure to migrate in the first place. Investing in rural areas, by improving roads, internet access and local industries, would give people realistic opportunities to earn a living without leaving their hometowns. Tax incentives could also encourage companies to relocate to smaller cities, which spreads economic growth more evenly.

In conclusion, rural-urban migration leads to housing shortages and overloaded public services in large cities. A combination of better urban planning and genuine investment in the countryside is the most effective way to tackle these problems.
samples.why: Clear position and logical organisation · main problems and measures extended with examples · good range of cohesive devices, one comma splice · less common vocabulary (informal settlements, relocate) · mostly accurate complex sentences.

samples.text:
Across much of the world, cities continue to swell as rural residents arrive in pursuit of work. Although this migration fuels economic growth, it frequently outpaces the capacity of urban areas to absorb newcomers, producing social and environmental strains that demand a coordinated policy response.

The most visible consequence is a crisis of housing. When population growth exceeds the rate of construction, prices rise beyond the reach of low-paid workers, who are pushed into overcrowded rented rooms or informal settlements on the urban fringe. These districts typically lack reliable water, sanitation and electricity, creating conditions in which disease spreads easily. A second set of problems stems from overstretched infrastructure. Transport networks designed for far smaller populations become gridlocked, lengthening commutes and worsening air quality, while schools and clinics struggle to meet demand. The result is a decline in living standards not only for migrants but for established residents too, which can in turn breed resentment between the two groups.

Tackling these difficulties requires measures both inside and outside the city. Within urban areas, governments should prioritise the construction of affordable housing and pair it with mass transit, so that new residential zones are connected to centres of employment rather than isolated from them. Upgrading informal settlements with basic services, rather than simply clearing them, is often a more humane and cost-effective approach. Equally important, however, is reducing the imbalance that drives migration in the first place. Investment in rural infrastructure, agricultural modernisation and regional industry can create viable livelihoods outside the major cities, while incentives for businesses to establish themselves in secondary towns would distribute economic opportunity more evenly.

In conclusion, rapid urban migration strains housing, transport and public services, lowering the quality of life for many residents. The most lasting solution lies in combining well-planned urban investment with a serious commitment to developing rural regions.
samples.why: Fully addresses both parts with well-developed, logically sequenced ideas · skilful cohesion and paragraphing · wide, precise vocabulary (outpaces, overstretched, viable livelihoods) · wide range of structures, essentially error-free.
